title: How a message becomes light
text:
You press send.
A fraction of a second later, someone else reads your message.
In between, for most of its journey, your message was not text at all.
It was light, travelling through a glass thread thinner than a hair.
This essay follows one tiny message on that journey: from the thing you typed, to numbers, to flashes of light, and back again.
To keep things clear, we will make one big simplification. The sender and the receiver are joined by a single fibre-optic cable. No routers, no exchanges, no undersea links. Just one strand of glass.
Even with that simplification, something interesting happens.

title: How a message becomes light
text:
Pick a message
Choose something small to send.
Each option is only a few bytes long, so we can follow every piece of it.


Code
viewof messageChoice = Inputs.radio(
  ["Hi", "👋", "8×8 icon"],
  {label: "Message", value: "Hi"}
)

title: How a message becomes light
How a message becomes light
How a message becomes light
text:
The drawing is a lie
There is a problem with the picture above.
It shows three wiggles of light per bit. The real number is very different.
Long-distance fibre links use infrared light with a wavelength of around 1550 nanometres. That light oscillates about 193 trillion times per second.
Even at a modest 10 billion bits per second, each bit lasts long enough for about 19,000 of those oscillations.


Code
viewof trueScale = Inputs.toggle({label: "Show one bit at true scale", value: false})









Code
LIGHT_FREQ_HZ = 299792458 / 1550e-9
BIT_RATE = 10e9
cyclesPerBit = LIGHT_FREQ_HZ / BIT_RATE

oneBit = trueScale
  ? []
  : d3.range(0, 1.0001, 1 / 400).map(t => ({t, y: Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * CARTOON_CYCLES * t)}))

Plot.plot({
  height: 160,
  marginLeft: 20,
  marginBottom: 40,
  style: {fontSize: "14px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "One bit (0.1 nanoseconds)", ticks: 0},
  y: {domain: [-1.2, 1.2], axis: null},
  marks: [
    trueScale
      ? Plot.areaY([{t: 0}, {t: 1}], {x: "t", y1: -1, y2: 1, fillOpacity: 0.85})
      : Plot.line(oneBit, {x: "t", y: "y", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {strokeOpacity: 0.2})
  ]
})







































Code
html`<p class="wm-muted">${trueScale
  ? `About ${Math.round(cyclesPerBit).toLocaleString("en-GB")} oscillations in this one bit. At this scale they merge into a solid band.`
  : `The cartoon: ${CARTOON_CYCLES} oscillations per bit.`}</p>`







So the wiggles in the rest of this essay are a cartoon.
What matters is the overall brightness in each bit slot, not the individual oscillations. That turns out to be exactly what the receiver measures.

title: How a message becomes light
How a message becomes light
text:
The receiver has to decide
Look at the third strip again.
The receiver never sees bits. It only sees a brightness that wobbles.
So once per bit, in the middle of each slot, it takes one measurement (the dots) and makes a decision:

above the dashed threshold, call it a 1;
below it, call it a 0.

On a short fibre this is trivially easy. The dots sit far from the line and every decision is right.
On a long fibre, the noise is large enough to push some dots across the line. The receiver cannot know that it happened. It simply makes the wrong call, and passes the wrong bit on.

title: How a message becomes light
text:
Two humps
One message is only a handful of bits, so it is a noisy way to judge a link.
Instead, imagine sending a few thousand random bits down the same fibre and plotting every measurement the receiver takes.


Code
N_HIST = 4000

histBits = (() => {
  const rand = mulberry32(99 + sendCount)
  return Array.from({length: N_HIST}, () => (rand() < 0.5 ? 0 : 1))
})()

histZ = gaussians(N_HIST, 4242 + 31 * sendCount)

histSamples = histBits.map((b, i) => {
  const y = b + noiseSd * histZ[i]
  return {sent: b ? "Laser was on (1)" : "Laser was off (0)", y, wrong: (y > 0.5 ? 1 : 0) !== b}
})

histWrong = histSamples.filter(d => d.wrong).length

halfWidth = Math.max(1.5, 4 * noiseSd)
histLo = 0.5 - halfWidth
histHi = 0.5 + halfWidth

Plot.plot({
  height: 300,
  marginLeft: 50,
  marginBottom: 45,
  style: {fontSize: "14px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {domain: [histLo, histHi], label: "Brightness measured at the centre of each bit"},
  y: {label: null, ticks: 0},
  color: {
    domain: ["Laser was off (0)", "Laser was on (1)"],
    range: ["#7f8c99", "#e8710a"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(
      histSamples.filter(d => d.y >= histLo && d.y <= histHi),
      Plot.binX(
        {y2: "count"},
        {x: "y", fill: "sent", thresholds: d3.range(histLo, histHi, (histHi - histLo) / 70), fillOpacity: 0.55}
      )
    ),
    Plot.ruleX([0.5], {strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})



































































Code
html`<p class="wm-muted">${histWrong} of ${N_HIST.toLocaleString("en-GB")} measurements landed on the wrong side of the threshold.</p>`







There are two humps: one for every time the laser was off, one for every time it was on.
Each hump has a width, set by the noise. The distance between them is set by the signal.
Errors are the parts of each hump that spill over the threshold into the other’s territory.
Engineers summarise this with a single number, the Q-factor: the gap between the two levels divided by the spread of the noise. In our simplified receiver,
\[
Q = \frac{\text{gap between the on and off levels}}{2 \times \text{noise spread}}
\]
and the fraction of bits that end up on the wrong side is
\[
\text{error rate} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
\]
A Q-factor of 6 gives about one error in a billion bits. For decades that was the classic target for a working link.

title: How a message becomes light
text:
The cliff
Every 15 km, the light halves. Because the noise stays fixed, the Q-factor halves too.
But the error rate does not halve. It explodes.
Drag the fibre length slowly from 100 km to 150 km. (This slider is linked to the one above.)


Code
Inputs.bind(
  Inputs.range([0, 200], {label: "Fibre length (km)", step: 1}),
  viewof distanceKm
)









Code
BER_FLOOR = 1e-15

berCurve = d3.range(60, 200.5, 0.5).map(km => {
  const q = Q_AT_REF * 10 ** (-ALPHA_DB_PER_KM * (km - REF_KM) / 10)
  return {km, ber: Math.max(BER_FLOOR, 0.5 * erfc(q / Math.SQRT2))}
})

Plot.plot({
  height: 320,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginBottom: 45,
  style: {fontSize: "14px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {domain: [60, 200], label: "Fibre length (km)"},
  y: {
    type: "log",
    domain: [BER_FLOOR, 1],
    label: "↑ Fraction of bits in error",
    ticks: [1e-15, 1e-12, 1e-9, 1e-6, 1e-3, 1],
    tickFormat: d => d === 1 ? "1" : `10${String(Math.round(Math.log10(d))).replace("-", "⁻").replace(/\d/g, c => "⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹"[c])}`,
    grid: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([1e-9], {strokeDasharray: "6,4", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.text([{km: 62, ber: 1e-9}], {x: "km", y: "ber", text: () => "Q = 6: one error in a billion", textAnchor: "start", dy: -9, fontSize: 12, fillOpacity: 0.8}),
    Plot.line(berCurve, {x: "km", y: "ber", strokeWidth: 2}),
    distanceKm >= 60
      ? Plot.dot([{km: distanceKm, ber: Math.max(BER_FLOOR, predictedBer)}], {x: "km", y: "ber", r: 6, fill: "#e8710a"})
      : null
  ]
})























For shorter fibres, the error rate is too small to draw. Then it climbs a wall.
Over the same 45 km in which the light merely fades to an eighth, the error rate goes from one in a billion to one in four:



Fibre length
Q-factor
Errors




100 km
6
about 1 in a billion


115 km
3
about 1 in 700


130 km
1.5
about 1 in 15


145 km
0.75
about 1 in 4



So a link does not fade gracefully, the way a radio station slowly turns to hiss.

A digital link works almost perfectly, until quite suddenly it does not.

That is why so much of optical engineering is about staying well away from the edge of that cliff, with margin to spare.

title: How a message becomes light
text:
What this simplifies
A real link is more complicated than the one on this page in almost every way. The main simplifications:

One fibre, no amplifiers. Long links put an optical amplifier every 80 km or so, boosting the light before it falls off the cliff. Each amplifier adds a little noise of its own.
No error correction. Real links add carefully designed redundant bits, so the receiver can find and fix most errors. A garbled “Hi” would usually be repaired before anyone saw it.
No packets or routing. On the real internet, your message is split into packets, wrapped in addresses, and passed between many links.
A perfect clock. We assumed the receiver knows exactly where each bit starts. Recovering that timing from the signal itself is a problem of its own.
A perfect laser. Real transmitters never switch fully off, and the pulses spread out as they travel (dispersion).
One kind of noise. We used fixed electronic noise only. Real receivers also have noise that grows with the signal.

The numbers are illustrative but realistic in scale: 1 mW of light launched, 0.2 dB of loss per kilometre, and receiver noise chosen so that Q = 6 at exactly 100 km.

title: How a message becomes light
section: One bit at a time is wasteful
text:
One bit at a time is wasteful
On–off keying sends one bit per time slot.
But light has more to it than brightness. It also has a phase, the point in its oscillation at any instant.
Long-distance links use both at once, packing several bits into every slot. That raises a new question: how close together can you pack the possibilities before noise starts confusing them?
That is the next essay.

title: There is no hidden text
text:
A watermark sounds like something added to a piece of text.
A hidden character. A tag. Some invisible metadata tucked between the words.
But statistical text watermarking can work without adding any of those things.
The text can look completely ordinary.
So where is the watermark?
In August 2026, Anthropic announced that future Claude models will carry a statistical watermark: a version of the SynthID-Text approach published by Google DeepMind.
Claude is the example that motivated this essay, but the idea is broader. Statistical watermarking can be applied to other language models too.
The interesting part is not simply that the text is marked.
It is how.

title: There is no hidden text
section: A language model is constantly making choices
text:
A language model is constantly making choices
A language model writes one token at a time.
At each step, there is usually not one uniquely correct continuation. Several words may fit.
Consider a deliberately simple example:

The weather today was cold and …



Code
nextWords = [
  {word: "grey", probability: 0.31},
  {word: "overcast", probability: 0.27},
  {word: "windy", probability: 0.19},
  {word: "wet", probability: 0.15},
  {word: "pleasant", probability: 0.07},
  {word: "sugary", probability: 0.01}
]

Plot.plot({
  height: 310,
  marginLeft: 90,
  marginBottom: 45,
  style: {
    fontSize: "14px",
    background: "transparent"
  },
  x: {
    domain: [0, 0.35],
    label: "Illustrative next-token probability",
    tickFormat: d => `${Math.round(d * 100)}%`
  },
  y: {
    domain: nextWords.map(d => d.word),
    label: null
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(nextWords, {
      x: "probability",
      y: "word",
      tip: false
    }),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
















The exact probabilities above are only illustrative.
The important point is the shape of the problem: some continuations are plausible, some are very unlikely, and several plausible choices may say essentially the same thing.
A watermark does not need to force the model to choose nonsense like sugary.
It can operate in the low-stakes choices between reasonable alternatives.

title: There is no hidden text
section: What a watermark can (and cannot) tell us
text:
What a watermark can (and cannot) tell us
A statistical watermark is evidence, not a visible stamp.
Its strength can depend on:

how much text there is;
how many watermark-bearing choices were available;
what happened to the text afterwards;
which watermarking scheme was used;
whether the verifier has access to the corresponding detection mechanism.

Even a positive detection does not necessarily settle conventional questions of authorship.
Claude might have generated an entire passage.
It might have heavily rewritten something written by a person.
Or it might have contributed only part of a larger document.
So the useful question is not simply:
Is this AI-generated?
It is closer to:

How much statistical evidence is there that this text passed through a particular generation process?

That is a much stranger kind of watermark.
There is no hidden text to find.
The evidence is distributed through the choices that created it.

title: There is no hidden text
text:
About this example
The interactive demo is a small, self-contained reconstruction, not Anthropic’s system.

Model: GPT-2 (openai-community/gpt2), sampling at temperature 0.8 and top-p 0.95, generating 180 tokens from eight short prompts.
Watermark: the SynthID-Text primitives built into Hugging Face Transformers, with the public example keys from its documentation, 5-token contexts and a 65,536-entry sampling table. Because the keys are public, anyone can verify this demo watermark. That is deliberate.
Detector: a logistic classifier on nine features, one per watermark key: the mean keyed g-value over the usable positions in a passage. It was trained on 40 ordinary and 40 watermarked passages, with a quarter held out. Held-out accuracy: % on about 20 passages, which is a sanity check rather than a benchmark.
Editing curve: the dashed line comes from replacing a growing fraction of words (0–50%) with words from a short fixed list. Real paraphrasing would disturb the text differently.
In your browser: the page loads only the GPT-2 tokenizer (via Transformers.js). The hashing and scoring were rewritten in JavaScript to match the Python implementation.

The “Strong / Moderate / Unclear / Weak” labels are thresholds I chose for readability. The score is not a calibrated probability that a passage was AI-generated.

title: About Kavit Tolia
text:
I studied mathematics at the University of Cambridge, then spent 12 years in asset management, working with quantitative models, data, uncertainty and investment portfolios.
Over time, I found myself increasingly drawn to the mathematics and mechanics underneath the decisions: how models represent the world, what information they capture, and where their assumptions begin to break down.
That curiosity eventually led me to step away from finance and pursue an MSc in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Science. My dissertation used simulation-based inference to estimate the properties of black-hole binaries from their gravitational-wave signals, which is where the black-hole degeneracy essay comes from.
I am now a PhD researcher at Queen Mary University of London, funded by EPSRC and supervised by Dr Paul Haigh and Dr Antonino Masaracchia. I work on autonomous optical networks: how reinforcement learning and generative AI agents can translate an operator’s plain-language intent into the decisions that run a fibre network.
I enjoy trying to understand technical ideas from first principles and finding ways to make their underlying structure easier to see. I do not think difficult subjects need to be made artificially simple, but I do think they can often be explained more clearly.
My current interests include reinforcement learning, scientific machine learning and inverse problems, and increasingly the physics of optical fibre, which is new to me. More broadly, I am interested in what models can learn from data, what remains unidentifiable, and how visualisation can help expose both the strengths and limitations of a model.
I am still learning, and I expect my understanding of many of these subjects to change. Part of the reason for building this site is to document that process.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
“This survey is anonymous.”
That sounds binary: either your identity is known, or it is not.
But anonymity is better thought of as a budget.
Every piece of information you reveal narrows the set of people you could be. Some answers spend very little of that budget. Others spend a lot.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
One bit at a time
A bit can be thought of as one perfectly chosen yes-or-no question that cuts the remaining group in half.
In a company of 500 people, there are only about nine halvings between the whole company and one person.
That does not mean nine survey questions will automatically identify you. Real surveys involve aggregation, imperfect information and organisational safeguards.
But it gives us a useful way to think about how quickly information accumulates.

title: Anonymity is not binary
Anonymity is not binary
text:
Rarity changes the cost
Not every answer reveals the same amount.
If half the company gives the same answer as you, that answer costs about one bit.
If only 1% of the company shares your answer, it reveals much more.
That means the same dropdown can have a very different anonymity cost for different respondents.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
Why demographics are difficult
Demographic information is often the most revealing part of a survey.
It is also often the information needed to detect inequities.
That creates a genuine tension: the groups whose experiences matter most to measure can also be the groups that are easiest to identify.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
What this does not mean
Being identifiable in principle is not the same as being identified, and being identified is not the same as being harmed.
Trust, governance, aggregation thresholds and organisational culture all matter.
The point is simpler: anonymity is not a switch. It is something that erodes as information accumulates.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
A useful consequence
If only a small minority raises an issue, the issue itself can become identifying information.
When more people raise the same genuine concern, that link weakens.
In that sense, anonymity can sometimes be strengthened collectively: when enough people say the true thing, no single voice stands out.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
What this calculator assumes
This is an illustration, not a re-identification tool.
The calculator assumes that the attributes you enter are independent, so it multiplies their population shares together. Real workplaces are messier: seniority, location, tenure and demographic characteristics can be correlated, sometimes strongly.
The resulting “people remaining” number should therefore be read as a simple expected count under that assumption, not as the number of people who could actually be identified.
It also ignores many things that matter in practice: aggregation thresholds, suppression of small groups, access controls, free-text responses, prior knowledge and the policies governing who can see the data.
The useful quantity here is the information revealed by a combination of answers, rather than a claim that a particular survey respondent can or will be identified.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime produced when massive objects accelerate.
Most of the time they are quite weak. But when compact objects such as black holes orbit one another, they can radiate enough energy in gravitational waves for those ripples to travel across the universe and eventually reach us.
As the two objects lose orbital energy, they spiral closer together. Their orbital motion speeds up, the gravitational-wave frequency rises, and eventually the objects merge.
The result is a characteristic waveform: a signal whose shape contains information about the system that produced it.
For massive black-hole binaries, those signals are expected to be particularly important for LISA, the planned space-based gravitational-wave observatory.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
Listening from space
Ground-based detectors such as LIGO observe gravitational waves at relatively high frequencies.
LISA will target much lower frequencies, around the millihertz regime, using three spacecraft separated by millions of kilometres. That makes it sensitive to systems that evolve on much longer timescales, including binaries containing massive black holes.
Some of these systems may be observed for days, weeks or even months as they spiral towards merger.
But detecting a gravitational wave is only the beginning.
What we really want to know is:

What kind of system produced it?

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
section: From a waveform to a black-hole binary
text:
From a waveform to a black-hole binary
A gravitational-wave signal is an observation of a source, not a direct description of it.
The waveform depends on many properties of the binary: the black-hole masses and spins, its distance from us, its orientation, its position on the sky and other parameters describing the system.
Inference works in the opposite direction.
We observe the waveform and ask which combinations of physical parameters could plausibly have produced it.
In practice, this is usually treated as a Bayesian inference problem.
Traditional approaches such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) explore the parameter space and build up a posterior distribution describing which source configurations are supported by the data.
More recently, simulation-based inference (SBI) methods use large collections of simulated gravitational-wave signals to learn parts of this inference process with neural networks.
The computational machinery can become sophisticated, but the underlying question remains simple:

Given the signal we measured, what can we actually learn about the source?

Those parameters are scientifically useful.
Masses and spins tell us about how black holes formed and grew. Distance and sky position tell us where the event occurred. Populations of many such systems can help us study the history of massive black holes and galaxy evolution, while sufficiently precise signals can also provide tests of gravity itself.
So recovering the source parameters accurately matters.
But there is a catch.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
section: When different sources look the same
text:
When different sources look the same
The mapping from source parameters to waveform is not always one-to-one.
Different combinations of parameters can sometimes produce remarkably similar observations.
That ambiguity is not necessarily a failure of the inference algorithm. It can be a property of the observation itself.
One particularly intuitive example involves:

luminosity distance, roughly how far away the binary is;
inclination, the angle at which we view its orbit.

Both affect the amplitude of the observed gravitational wave.
A more distant binary appears weaker. But changing the orientation of the system can also change the amplitude.
That creates the possibility of a trade-off: could a binary be farther away but oriented in such a way that its waveform still looks almost the same?

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
One waveform, many possible sources
Suppose we observe a waveform from a binary at:

luminosity distance: 1000 Mpc
inclination: 1.05 rad

We can then ask a simple inverse question:

What other combinations of distance and inclination could have produced something very similar?

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
A valley of possible answers
The important feature is the valley.
Moving distance and inclination together can keep the waveform close to the reference. Rather than pointing to one unique solution, the observation is compatible with a family of nearby parameter combinations.
The inverse map is therefore not one-to-one.
Different physical systems can occupy different places in parameter space while producing nearly the same observation.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
The lesson for machine learning
A sufficiently flexible model can learn extremely complicated mappings from data.
But better prediction machinery does not automatically make an inverse problem identifiable.
If the observations supplied to a model contain almost the same signal for two different source configurations, distinguishing those configurations becomes intrinsically difficult.
A larger neural network does not make that information suddenly appear.
The useful question is therefore not only:
Can the model predict the parameters?
but also:
Which parameters are actually identifiable from the information we have measured?

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
Can the degeneracy be broken?
Sometimes.
A degeneracy does not necessarily mean that the parameters are fundamentally unknowable. It means that the information we are currently using does not distinguish them cleanly enough.
More information can change that.
Richer waveform structure.
Real gravitational-wave signals contain more than a single amplitude pattern. Higher-order modes, spin-induced precession and other waveform features depend on the source parameters in different ways. Those additional structures can help distinguish systems that otherwise appear similar.
The detector response.
LISA will not observe a source from one fixed viewpoint. As the spacecraft constellation moves around the Sun, its response to the source changes. That time-dependent information can help constrain source orientation and sky position, reducing some degeneracies.
Independent observations.
If an electromagnetic counterpart or host galaxy can be identified, external information may provide additional constraints on quantities such as sky position or distance.
Representing the ambiguity properly.
Some degeneracy may remain even after all available information is included. In that case the solution is not to force the inference algorithm to produce one answer. The posterior should retain the range, correlation or multiple modes that remain compatible with the observation.
That is an important part of scientific inference.
Uncertainty is not always something an algorithm has failed to remove.
Sometimes it is telling us something real about what the data can and cannot distinguish.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
About this example
This is deliberately a simplified illustration of the distance–inclination degeneracy rather than a full LISA parameter-estimation analysis.
The waveforms here were generated with PyCBC using IMRPhenomXHM. The comparison uses the plus polarisation and a simple amplitude-sensitive relative difference between waveforms.
A realistic LISA analysis would also include the detector response, instrumental noise, additional source parameters and a proper likelihood or posterior calculation.
The point of the example is therefore not that these particular parameter combinations would remain indistinguishable in a complete LISA analysis. It is to show how parameter degeneracies arise when different physical configurations map to very similar observations.
